items.content:
[This article was first published on R Works, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)

Data centers required to fuel the ambitions of Artificial Intelligence companies have sparked a nationwide conversation. AI companies are moving quickly to build out infrastructure and local communities are pushing back to resist what they see as the appropriation of public resources such as electricity and water to further enrich wealthy corporations. Moreover, the sentiment shared by both the political left and right is that data centers will significantly degrade the quality of life for those living adjacent to a data center and to the extended community as well. This post implements a non-trivial Bayesian Network to study the risks involved. I hope it is of some interest to a broad audience including, people interested in clarifying their thoughts about the risks that data centers may pose to their particular community and analysts curious about Bayesian Networks. However, I think the sample model built out in this post will be especially interesting to decision analysts who know quite a bit about Bayesian Networks but may be unfamiliar with the R programming language and unaware that there is capable opensource software which can provide capabilities beyond those offered by proprietary software systems.

Other than addressing the topic of data center risks the analysis contains no original research except perhaps the contribution of ChatGPT 5.6 Luna which conjured up the innovative parts of the synthetic data generation algorithm from a series of requirements.

Data Center Risks

Rational discussion about the perceived risks associated with the construction of data centers could benefit from a disciplined approach to organizing information and opinions into risk a analysis flexible enough to the consequences of complex interactions among risk factors. The Bayesian Network presented in this post is intended to be first step towards building such a tool.

In general, the risks imposed by data centers fall into the following general categories. See Appendix C below for some references to investigative reporting supporting these risk categories.

  • Electricity. A data center’s power demand can affect the immediate substation, the regional transmission system, and electricity rates for customers across a utility territory. The key questions are who pays for new generation and transmission, whether the facility has a dedicated rate, and whether its demand is flexible during shortages.

  • Water. Water use depends heavily on cooling design, climate, server load, and the use of reclaimed water. The relevant impact area is often the watershed rather than the property boundary. During droughts, a data center may compete with households, agriculture, industry, and ecosystems.

  • Land and housing. The facility itself may occupy hundreds of acres when parking, substations, cooling systems, security setbacks, and transmission corridors are included. Construction can remove farmland or open space, while the associated workforce and infrastructure can increase housing demand.

  • Noise and air quality. The most immediate quality-of-life impacts are usually construction activity, cooling-system noise, transformer hum, generator testing, lighting, and occasional diesel emissions. These effects decline with distance but can remain significant for nearby homes, schools, and outdoor spaces.

  • Grid reliability and affordability. A data center can bring grid upgrades that improve regional infrastructure, but rapid demand growth can also strain generation and transmission. If costs are not assigned directly to the facility, residential and small-business customers may absorb part of them.

  • Governance and fairness. The distance framework should be paired with an equity analysis: who receives jobs, tax revenue, and infrastructure improvements, and who experiences noise, land loss, water competition, higher rates, or pollution? Community-benefit agreements, transparent resource-demand disclosures, enforceable noise and water standards, and clear cost-recovery rules can substantially change the outcome.

Potential Benefits

Supporters of data centers emphasize the potential benefits of building a data center. These may include increased tax revenue and increased temporary employment. However, most of the reporting referenced below indicates that they do not compensate for the risks.

Organizing the risks and benefits

Model building begins by organizing nodes into a a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with arrows pointing from root nodes which are thought to drive other nodes that represent factors that intensify risk. Eventually the information in these nodes flow to nodes which quantify different kinds of risk. Finally the information from the risk nodes flow into a node that quantifies overall community risk. The following graph expands on the general categories listed above, enumerates a number of risk factors with arrows indicating the direction influence or causality. The names of the nodes are for the most part self explanatory. Note that the scale of the data center and distance from the data center are fundamental factors driving risk.

The number of nodes in this graph are probably much larger than would be required for an exploratory mode. However, I have elected to go with the larges list that seemed to me to be reasonable and coherent in order to provide an example that is more complex than a typical “toy” mode. And since it is usually much easier to remove code than add it, the model below should be useful in deriving a more parsimonious custom model.

The DAG

The code below builds a discrete Bayesian Network based on the above directed acyclic graph using bnlearn package.

Required packages and helper functions 
# ============================================================
# Bayesian Network for Data-Center Community Risk
# ============================================================

# Install packages once if necessary:
# install.packages(c("bnlearn", "ggplot2"))

library(ggplot2)
library(Rgraphviz)
library(igraph)

}

Some DAG Statistics

There are a few statistics that may provide some insight into the structure of a Bayesian Network.

Average Markov Blanket Size

In a Bayesian network, a Markov blanket of a target variable consists of the variable’s parent nodes, child nodes, and spouses child nodes, the other parents of the children. These are the nodes that determine the target variables behavior. In general a smaller value for average Markov blanket size indicates a sparse network and lower computational complexity (the computational power required for probabilistic inference)

Average Branching Factor

The branching factor of a node is equal to the number of direct children. The Average Branching Factor is the total number of directed edges divided by the total number of nodes. This may be interpreted as the average spread of downstream influence.

Average Neighborhood Size

The neighborhood of a node consists of both its direct parents and its direct children, treating the graph as undirected. Average neighborhood size is the average number of incoming and outgoing connections.

This block of codes computes these statistics, which may be useful in comparing variations of the network.

Network Statistics Calculations 
#library(bnlearn)

# dag should be a bnlearn network created with model2network(),
# empty.graph(), hc(), tabu(), gs(), etc.

node_names <- nodes(dag)

# Markov blanket size for each node
markov_blanket_sizes <- sapply(
  node_names,
  function(node) {

)

# Direct neighbours = parents + children
neighbourhood_sizes <- sapply(
  node_names,
  function(node) {
    direct_neighbours <- unique(c(
      parents(dag, node),
      children(dag, node)
    ))
    
    length(direct_neighbours)
  }
)

branching_factors <- sapply(
  node_names,
  function(node) {

Synthetic Data

This code implements a custom structural risk-propagation simulator to generate synthetic data based on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), estimates for the discrete probability distributions foverning the root nodes and influencer nodes, estimates of initial risk scores. Instead of relying on traditional Conditional Probability Tables this architecture utilizes a continuous, score-based risk-mapping framework. The simulation engine evaluates the nodes observation-by-observation in a strict topological ordering (parents before children). For each node, it calculates a localized Target Risk Score bounded between 0 and 1 (where 0 represents lowest risk/exposure and 1 represents highest). It then converts this target risk into discrete state probabilities using an exponential distance formula. This allows the network to linearly model highly complex, multi-parent conditional relationships.

Structure of the Data Generator

The data generation algorithm divides the DAG nodes into two distinct behavioral categories based on how their state-to-risk mappings are handled:

Node Type Definition & Purpose Code Implementation
Direct Nodes Baseline operational variables that have specific impacts on risk. Their states do not follow a uniform scale. Protective variables (like EconomicBenefit or AccessToBenefits) map inversely, where high values equal low risk. Explicitly Mapped inside create_risk_mappings() via custom, hand-tuned numeric vectors (e.g., Distance = c(Adjacent = 1.00, Neighborhood = 0.80, …)).
Derived Nodes Downstream environmental, social, infrastructure, or ultimate risk outcomes. They track consecutive intensities or severities that naturally follow a uniform logical progression from safe to severe. Dynamically Populated using a single, reusable standard_mapping array (Low = 0.15, Moderate = 0.50, High = 0.85) iterated over a list of standard_risk_nodes.

Prior probabilities are only assigned to root states (states that have no parents). For non-root (child) nodes, the distributions of probabilities for states like “Low”, “Moderate”, and “High” are not static. These are generated dynamically for every single row using a 4-step pipeline that maps parental risk onto an exponential distance curve.

Step 1: Compress Parent States into a Single Risk Score

The code looks at the already-generated states of the child’s parents in the current row. It translates those text states into numeric risk values using create_risk_mappings() and calculates a weighted average:

For each child node risk assignment:

  • Random Gaussian noise is injected
  • The final value is forced to stay within the strict logical bounds:

The probabilities for the child states are set as follows. The code calculates how far each possible child state’s predefined risk score (e.g., , , ) is from the dynamic calculated in Step 2. It runs these distances through a Laplacian radial kernel.:

Data Generator Code

The following code implements the code to generate the data, and contains the default values for the probabilities of root node distributions of “Low”, “Moderate” and “High” risk and default values for risk estimates.

Show the code 
# ================================================================
# Synthetic data generation from a bnlearn DAG
# ================================================================

#library(bnlearn)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# Main function
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
generate_synthetic_data <- function(
  n = 10000, 
  global_risk_shift = 0.00, 
  parent_effect_strength = 1.00, 
  conditional_noise = 0.10
) {
  # ARCHITECTURAL NOTE: Dynamic environment lookup lets the function bypass bnlearn's 
  # restrictive function signatures while maintaining access to the global network structure.
  if (!exists("dag", envir = parent.frame(), inherits = TRUE)) {
    stop("An object named 'dag' must exist before calling generate_synthetic_data().")
  }
  dag <- get("dag", envir = parent.frame(), inherits = TRUE)
  
  # Structural defensive validation steps
  validate_dag(dag)
  validate_generator_arguments(n, global_risk_shift, parent_effect_strength, conditional_noise)
  
  # Bundle configurations into a centralized configuration object
  config <- create_network_config(
    n = n, 
    global_risk_shift = global_risk_shift, 
    parent_effect_strength = parent_effect_strength, 
    conditional_noise = conditional_noise
  )
  
  # Execute the core simulation pipeline
  generate_rows_from_dag(dag = dag, config = config)
}

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# Generate all observations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
generate_rows_from_dag <- function(dag, config) {
  if (!is.null(config$seed)) { set.seed(config$seed) }
  
  dag_nodes <- bnlearn::nodes(dag)
  
  # CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL STEP: Nodes must be sorted topologically. 
  # This guarantees a parent node has simulated data before a child tries to read it.
  generation_order <- get_topological_order(dag)
  
  validate_configuration(dag = dag, dag_nodes = dag_nodes, config = config)
  
  # OPTIMIZATION: Memory pre-allocation prevents R from copying data frames repeatedly in memory loops.
  result <- setNames(vector("list", length(dag_nodes)), dag_nodes)
  for (node in dag_nodes) {
    result[[node]] <- character(config$n)
  }
  
  # Row-by-row simulation loop
  for (i in seq_len(config$n)) {
    one_row <- generate_one_observation(dag = dag, generation_order = generation_order, config = config)
    for (node in dag_nodes) {
      result[[node]][i] <- one_row[[node]]
    }
  }
  
  # Formatting raw arrays back into structured, clean R Factor columns
  result <- as.data.frame(result, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
  for (node in dag_nodes) {
    result[[node]] <- factor(result[[node]], levels = config$states[[node]])
  }
  result
}

generate_one_observation <- function(dag, generation_order, config) {
  row <- setNames(vector("list", length(generation_order)), generation_order)
  
  # Sequentially process each node down the causal chain
  for (node in generation_order) {
    node_states <- config$states[[node]]
    node_parents <- bnlearn::parents(dag, node)
    
    # ROOT NODE INTERCEPT: If a node has no parents, sample from its static baseline distribution.
    if (length(node_parents) == 0) {
      probabilities <- config$root_probabilities[[node]]
      probabilities <- probabilities[node_states]
      probabilities <- normalize_probabilities(probabilities)
      names(probabilities) <- node_states
      row[[node]] <- sample_state(probabilities)
      next
    }
    
    # CHILD NODE COMPUTATION: Compress multi-parent states into a singular continuous score
    parent_risk <- calculate_parent_risk(parents = node_parents, row = row, config = config)
    
    # LINEAR SENSITIVITY TRANSFORM: Shifts values relative to a 0.5 mid-point based on network effects strength
    conditional_risk <- 0.5 + config$parent_effect_strength * (parent_risk - 0.5)
    
    # Map the scalar risk target back into a probability distribution across discrete states
    probabilities <- calculate_state_probabilities(
      node = node, states = node_states, 
      conditional_risk = conditional_risk, config = config
    )
    row[[node]] <- sample_state(probabilities)
  }
  row
}

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# Parent-risk calculations

## ----------------------------------------------------------------
calculate_parent_risk <- function(parents, row, config) {
## Extract configured or default (1.00) relative weights for each parent
parent_weights <- vapply(parents, function(parent) {
get_parent_weight(parent = parent, config = config)
}, numeric(1))
## Convert each parent's current simulated text state into its corresponding numeric risk score
weighted_scores <- vapply(seq_along(parents), function(i) {
parent <- parents[[i]]
parent_score <- state_risk_score(node = parent, state = row[[parent]], config = config)
parent_score * parent_weights[[i]]
}, numeric(1))
## COMPRESSION METRIC: Calculated as a weighted average to safely scale multi-parent risks between 0 and 1
sum(weighted_scores) / sum(parent_weights)
}
get_parent_weight <- function(parent, config) {
weights <- config$parent_weights
## Defensive safety check guarding against structural mismatches between the input DAG and configuration vectors
if (is.null(weights) || is.null(names(weights)) || !parent %in% names(weights)) {
return(1.00)
}
weight <- unname(weights[[parent]])
if (!is.finite(weight) || weight < 0) {
stop("The weight for parent '", parent, "' must be a finite, non-negative number.")
}
weight
}
## ----------------------------------------------------------------## Conditional probability calculations## ----------------------------------------------------------------
calculate_state_probabilities <- function(node, states, conditional_risk, config) {
## STOCHASTIC PERTURBATION: Incorporates systemic shifts (scenarios) and random environmental noise via Gaussian distributions.
target_risk <- conditional_risk + config$global_risk_shift + rnorm(n = 1, mean = 0, sd = config$conditional_noise)
## Hard boundaries preventing mathematically invalid probabilities outside (0, 1)
target_risk <- max(0.01, min(target_risk, 0.99))
state_scores <- vapply(states, function(state) {
state_risk_score(node = node, state = state, config = config)
}, numeric(1) )
## EXPONENTIAL DISTANCE KERNEL (RBF-style): States whose static risk mappings sit closest## to the dynamic target_risk calculation receive exponentially higher generation probabilities.
concentration <- 6
probabilities <- exp(-concentration * abs(state_scores - target_risk))
## Convert distances to a standard, valid probability array summing to 1.00
probabilities <- normalize_probabilities(probabilities)
names(probabilities) <- states
probabilities
}
state_risk_score <- function(node, state, config) {
mapping <- config$risk_mappings[[node]]
if (is.null(mapping)) { stop("No risk mapping is defined for node '", node, "'.") }
if (!state %in% names(mapping)) { stop("No risk score is defined for node '", node, "' and state '", state, "'.") }
unname(mapping[[state]])
}
normalize_probabilities <- function(probabilities) {
probabilities <- pmax(probabilities, 0)
if (length(probabilities) == 0) { stop("Cannot normalize an empty probability vector.") }
## Uniform fallback handling to preserve math stability if all states evaluate to a zero score
if (sum(probabilities) == 0) {
probabilities <- rep(1 / length(probabilities), length(probabilities))
} else {
probabilities <- probabilities / sum(probabilities)
}
probabilities
}
sample_state <- function(probabilities) {
## Executes a standard weighted random draw based on the dynamically formulated distribution
sample(x = names(probabilities), size = 1, prob = probabilities)
}

validate_dag <- function(dag) {
if (!inherits(dag, "bn")) { stop("dag must be a bnlearn network object with class 'bn'.") }
}
validate_generator_arguments <- function(n, global_risk_shift, parent_effect_strength, conditional_noise) {
if (length(n) != 1 || !is.numeric(n) || is.na(n) || n < 1 || n != as.integer(n)) { stop("n must be one positive integer.") }
numeric_values <- c(global_risk_shift, parent_effect_strength, conditional_noise)
if (any(!is.numeric(numeric_values)) || any(!is.finite(numeric_values))) { stop("global_risk_shift, parent_effect_strength, and conditional_noise must be finite numeric values.") }

validate_configuration <- function(dag, dag_nodes, config) {
missing_states <- setdiff(dag_nodes, names(config$states))
if (length(missing_states) > 0) { stop("No state definitions supplied for: ", paste(missing_states, collapse = ", ")) }
root_nodes <- dag_nodes[vapply(dag_nodes, function(node) { length(bnlearn::parents(dag, node)) == 0 }, logical(1))]
missing_root_probabilities <- setdiff(root_nodes, names(config$root_probabilities))
if (length(missing_root_probabilities) > 0) { stop("No root probabilities supplied for: ", paste(missing_root_probabilities, collapse = ", ")) }
missing_mappings <- setdiff(dag_nodes, names(config$risk_mappings))
if (length(missing_mappings) > 0) { stop("No risk mappings supplied for: ", paste(missing_mappings, collapse = ", ")) }
}
get_topological_order <- function(dag) {
## KAHN'S ALGORITHM EXTENSION: Resolves dependence hierarchies.## Iteratively extracts nodes whose parents have already crossed the resolution boundary.
dag_nodes <- bnlearn::nodes(dag)
remaining_nodes <- dag_nodes
ordering <- character(0)
while (length(remaining_nodes) > 0) {
available_nodes <- remaining_nodes[vapply(remaining_nodes, function(node) {
node_parents <- bnlearn::parents(dag, node)
all(node_parents %in% ordering)
}, logical(1))]
# If no nodes are free but un-generated items remain, a cyclic loop exists.
if (length(available_nodes) == 0) {
stop("The graph does not appear to be acyclic, or its parent relationships could not be resolved.")
}
available_nodes <- sort(available_nodes)
ordering <- c(ordering, available_nodes)
remaining_nodes <- setdiff(remaining_nodes, available_nodes)
}
ordering
}

Summary

This post presents a model that is intended to serve as a template for building Bayesian Networks to explore the risk posed to a community from building a data center. It implements R code that includes a robust DAG, a synthetic data generator that can be customized to reflect the initial probability distributions and risk intensity settings. In a modeling effort for a particular community, these could be elicited from community experts, tables and visualizations to evaluate multiple risk states.

We human beings are notoriously bad at intuitively arriving at the correct logical conclusions to even the simplest conditional probability arguments. It is envisioned that main use of tool implemented in this post would be to help people organize their beliefs about the risks of building a data center in their community in a way that would enable them to test their assumptions and explore the probable consequences.

          stringsAsFactors = FALSE

    }

Appendix B: The Laplacian Radial Kernel

This code plots the Laplacian radial kernel used to set risk for derived, non-root nodes in the algorithm to generate synthetic data.

across our three standard derived states (Low = 0.15, Moderate = 0.50, High = 0.85). It dynamically plots how the final normalized probabilities shift as the calculated Target Risk moves from 0.00 to 1.00.

Child-state probabilities were generated using normalized exponential distance weights. For each state, the weight was defined as above where is the predefined risk score for state s. is the parent-dependent target risk, and c controls concentration around the target. This is equivalent to applying a one-dimensional exponential, or Laplacian, radial kernel centered at , followed by normalization across child states.

Show the code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Define Core Simulation Parameters
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
concentration <- 6
state_scores  <- c(Low = 0.15, Moderate = 0.50, High = 0.85)
target_range  <- seq(0.00, 1.00, by = 0.01)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Compute Normalized Probabilities over Target Risk Continuum
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
plot_data <- data.frame()

for (target_risk in target_range) {
  # Step 3: Measure raw exponential distances
  raw_probs <- exp(-concentration * abs(state_scores - target_risk))
  
  # Step 4: Normalize scores to sum to 1.00
  final_probs <- raw_probs / sum(raw_probs)
  
  # Bind results for plotting
  row_df <- data.frame(
    TargetRisk = target_risk,
    Low        = final_probs["Low"],
    Moderate   = final_probs["Moderate"],
    High       = final_probs["High"]
  )
  plot_data <- rbind(plot_data, row_df)
}

Appendix C: Some Documentation on Data Center Risks

This section provides some references, mostly investigative reports, that support the general risk categories used in the model.

Electricity, Grid Reliability, and Affordability

  • Earthjustice reports that the traditional utility model socializes grid infrastructure costs across the entire customer base. When utilities race to build new substations, gas power plants, and transmission lines for tech facilities, standard ratepayers often absorb those costs.

  • CEPR economic analysis found that adding a single average hyperscale facility increases local residential power prices by roughly 4%, while adding ten facilities spikes residential rates by 13%.

Brookings Institution research warns that rapid large-load data center growth is decoupling electricity bills from baseline inflation, compounding utility disconnection rates in high-density clusters like Northern Virginia. Nuance/Counter-Perspective: A working paper

Water Resource Demands

  • A hydrologist report from North Carolina State University sates that data centers rely heavily on “open-loop evaporative cooling” systems that consume water and release it as vapor instead of returning it to the local system. Emphasizing that because data center demand “never sleeps,” it permanently removes millions of gallons daily and alters the baseline natural water balance of watersheds.

  • Ceres Sustainability Report predicts that “in the coming years, annual water use associated with data center electricity consumption is expected to increase by 400%, from an estimated 2.9 billion gallons to over 14.5 billion gallons – enough to supply the entire city of Scottsdale, Ariz. for over 2 years and that increases regional water stress by up to 17% annually in already strained basins.

  • The Next 10 report: The Intersection of Data Center Development, Water Availability, and Environmental Justice in California discusses the potential impact of data centers to California communities that are suffering water shortages and concludes among its top 1 findings that: “Water scarcity impacts extend beyond the footprint of any single data center, particularly when facilities rely on imported water or shared groundwater basins”

Land and Housing

  • According to the report From Energy Use to Air Quality, the Many Ways Data Centers Affect US Communities a national evaluation by the World Resources Institute (WRI), the average footprint of a modern data center footprint spans approximately 224 acres (roughly 450 football fields). Data centers often encroach into rural-zoned lands or agricultural areas.

  • The Brookings Institute report New evidence on data center employment effects claims that wages are unaffected by data center builds while home prices rise 2%-5%.

Noise and Air Quality and Environmental Polution

  • An investigative report by The Guardian exposed instances where tech developers skirted stringent clean air regulations by splitting massive facility configurations into multiple “minor” emission sources on paper to fast-track permitting.

  • The IEEE Report We Need to Talk About AI’s Impact on Public Health Data-center pollution is linked to asthma, heart attacks, and more outlines a number of way that data centers adversely affect public health. For example, data center backup generators run on diesel fuel and emit 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than an equivalent natural gas power plant.

  • The December 2024 report issued by the Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC), Data Centers in Virginia (Report 598) found that:

    • about one-third of operational data center properties in Virginia sit within 200 feet of residential zoned properties.
    • data centers emit a continuous, low-frequency hum generated by around-the-clock cooling infrastructure, HVAC systems, and mechanical fans. Because low-frequency sound waves travel further and penetrate residential structures more efficiently than higher-frequency sounds, they frequently trigger complaints regarding well-being and disrupted sleep patterns from nearby families

Governance and Fairness

The World Resources Institute Report cited above Using the Centers for Disease Control’s (CDC) Environmental Justice Index, the World Resources Institute proved that a disproportionate percentage of data center developments cluster in census tracts that suffer from above-median pre-existing environmental vulnerabilities (such as high baseline air pollution) and social vulnerabilities (such as lower average education and higher poverty rates).

items.content:
[This article was first published on Seascapemodels, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

Claude Code (and many other agents) has been getting so good at ecological analysis that I find I’m increasingly tempted not to directly review the code it writes. In fact, it finds more mistakes in my code than I find in its code these days.

So I need a way to check the validity of the code it writes. Here’s the strategy for this I’ve been developing. Its a work in progress.

Specification

Start with a clear written specification for the data analysis or modelling. This should include equations for the modelling. This ensures I understand what I want the analysis to do (even if its not what I get initially).

Claude is very helpful at this stage to review it for logical errors.

Adversarial code review

This is a no brainer. Use the agent, or ideally another provider’s agent, to review the code for errors.

Data processing checks

Instruct Claude to check all data processing steps and fail loudly if inconsistencies are found. That’s probably sufficient these days, but if you want to be thorough you can think about what you need at each stage and tell it to check for that.

For example, make sure the final dataframe used in the model has N rows, or that the number of unique survey IDs == the number of rows in the dataframe.

There are various R packages to support this like pointblank and validate.

Testing against simulated data with known truth

Often in ecology we are fitting generative models, that is, you can simulate data right out of the model you are fitting. So invert your specification of the model to be a specification that simulates data with a known model. Then run the simulated data through your workflow to see if it recovers the known parameters.

If you are doing probabilistic inference you can also check other common verification statistics like coverage (the 95% CIs should cover the point estimate in 95% of randomized datasets).

Create the data simulation in a separate Claude and R environment, to ensure independence. Make sure the AI memory storage options are turned off, or set to incognito mode, to ensure no leakage of information through memory files too.

There are also many data simulation functions as R packages or within R packages. For instance, many advanced modelling packages also provide a simulation function. You can use these to further reduce the chances of errors in your simulation step

Other simulation tests

You can also do checks where you muddle the real data directly and run it through your workflow. For instance, you should get the same result if you reshuffle rows of your data-frame randomly.

If you reshuffle values in the covariate columns independently of the response, then the effects of covariate should be 0 on average. If your workflow is about model selection, then enforcing shared rank ordering of a covariate and the response you should (almost certainly) find that covariate pops up in every model selected by the AIC.

Test multiple methods

In the simplest case, the same model fitted with different implementations should return the same results. For example compare results from lmer lme and glmmTMB. You can get claude to fire up sub-agents to write a script for each one independently.

In more complex cases it can still be useful to do fit different models and compare results, even in the models have slightly different meanings. This may reveal errors, but it may also reveal places where your model assumptions are not robust. For instance, do different model selection methods result in the same model?

What’s next?

Part of the problem is that once you start using an agent it will write very complex R code. Claude Code has this obsession with making absolutely generalizable scripts. For instance, it commonly writes functions just to identify the root file path for a key data file.

The other part of its complexity is adding numerous print statements to the R scripts, so it can see intermediate results in the terminal output. I normally do these interactively so they stay out of my scripts.

All this extra code means it becomes even more tedious to review its work. Its like a double edged sword, the agent is powerful, but it makes more review work.

So its clear to me that we soon won’t bother reading the code they write. That means we need to adapt how we approach coding and data analysis, and especially ensure we have checks in place that we understand the code we are producing and understand its correct.

This list is my start at that.

Send a comment if you have other suggestions for ways to test code written by agents.
